title: SORA: Free Second-Order Attacks in Fast Adversarial Training
claim: Training drifts from a smooth, near-linear loss surface to a nonlinear one that fools single-step attacks and exposes weaknesses that stronger attacks exploit.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right progression, dashed dividers, shared color legend and attack key
description: Three circular top-down maps of a loss surface, ordered left to right and titled Robust State, Near CO and After CO. A diverging color scale runs from blue (confidently correct) through pale yellow (uncertain) to red (confidently wrong). In the left panel the blue region is one smooth ellipse. In the middle panel a small bump and a ring of yellow appear around the center. In the right panel concentric rings of blue and red form around the sample, with a blue pocket above it. A black dot marks the sample. Colored arrows from the dot show the perturbations of each attack. Brown is FGSM, purple is FGSM-RS, yellow is NFGSM, orange is our method, and green dotted multi-step paths are PGD. A legend sits at the top right and a color bar at the left. The eye goes first to the colorful concentric rings and the arrows.
caption: Evolution of the loss landscape geometry around a sample during FGSM training. Left: Early in training, before CO, the model is robust, with FGSM and PGD accuracies closely matched. The loss surface is approximately semilinear. Middle: A few batch updates before CO, the decision boundary begins to wrap around the original and adversarial examples, forming a nonlinear region that is not yet misclassified. Right: This nonlinearity escalates, leading to misclassification in that region, which stronger attacks such as PGD exploit. Perturbations from other attacks and our method (SORA) are also visualized.
abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is a leading defense against adversarial examples but often suffers from Catastrophic Overfitting (CO) in efficient single-step variants, where robustness to multi-step attacks collapses despite high single-step performance. We address this failure mode with two contributions. First, we formalize Epsilon Overfitting (EO), a perspective in which fixed perturbation magnitudes and directions exacerbate CO, and show that introducing perturbation variability significantly improves robust generalization across different architectures and datasets. Second, we propose PertAlign (Perturbation Alignment), a theoretically grounded, computationally negligible metric that predicts CO onset by measuring gradient alignment across attack stages. Leveraging these insights, we introduce SORA, an adaptive step-size AT method that dynamically adjusts perturbations based on loss surface geometry. SORA consistently prevents CO, achieves state-of-the-art robustness and clean accuracy, and generalizes across datasets and architectures using a single fixed set of hyperparameters, which is essential for applicability in fast AT. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets and architectures show that SORA matches or surpasses the robustness of prior methods while delivering higher clean accuracy and superior efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/SecondOrderAT/SORA.
